Som Crisis: Kyrgyzstan Grapples with Rapid Currency Devaluation, Economic Turmoil

BISHKEK – Kyrgyzstan is facing a deepening economic crisis as the national currency, the som, has sharply depreciated over the past two weeks, sending shockwaves through businesses and households across the country. The situation remains volatile, with the exchange rate surpassing 110 soms to the US dollar on Thursday, compared to 89 soms at the start of the month.

The sudden collapse of the som has led to rising prices on imported goods, fuel, and daily necessities, causing widespread concern among citizens. “We are seeing bread prices up 20 percent in just one week. People are coming in worried that tomorrow it will be even higher,” said Aizada Sarybaeva, manager of a Bishkek grocery market. Currency exchange points in the capital have reported long queues as residents rush to buy dollars or euros, fearing further declines.

Kyrgyzaltyn OJSC, the state-owned gold mining and trading company, is among the firms affected by the currency crisis. In a statement released Thursday, the company confirmed operational difficulties due to the volatility of the som and interruptions in imported equipment supplies. “Our costs have increased significantly in recent days, particularly for spare parts and chemicals sourced from abroad. We are working to maintain production but face serious challenges,” the statement read.

The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic has intervened several times this week, selling foreign currency reserves in an attempt to stabilize the som. However, analysts warn that the interventions have had limited effect so far. “The pressures are both external and internal: regional trade disruptions and a decrease in remittance inflows are putting immense strain on the currency,” explained economist Timur Abdrakhmanov. He added that the government’s options are narrowing as reserves dwindle.

Other sectors are also feeling the impact. At the Dordoi wholesale market, traders reported sluggish sales and difficulties restocking inventory. “Our suppliers from Kazakhstan and China are demanding payment in dollars. With the som so weak, many of us can’t afford to buy new stock,” said trader Bakytbek Kadyrov.

The government has convened emergency meetings with business leaders and international partners, but has yet to announce a concrete recovery plan. “We are monitoring the situation closely and will take all necessary measures to ensure stability,” Finance Minister Aibek Kenzhebaev told reporters.

With the crisis still unfolding, uncertainty remains high in Kyrgyzstan’s markets and households, as citizens brace for further economic turbulence.
